{"id": "49:13/q02", "question": "Who or what are the male and female?", "turns_on": "Whether the pair denotes common ancestors, each person's parents, or only male biological material.", "positions": [{"id": "49:13/q02/p1", "position": "Adam and Eve, the shared first parents.", "reasons": "Al-Qurṭubī compares 4:1; common descent refutes lineage pride. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī and al-Ālūsī find this stronger when that is the point."}, {"id": "49:13/q02/p2", "position": "Each person has a father and mother and is made from both parents' fluids.", "reasons": "Mujāhid cites this verse for both fluids. Al-Qurṭubī uses 86:6–7, resemblance from both, and the meeting waters of 54:12; verses mentioning one drop do not make it male only. Asad stresses equal human dignity. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī prefers the broader reading where all class distinctions are addressed. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī reports an objection that wider class equality does not follow from a specific condemnation of lineage."}, {"id": "49:13/q02/p3", "position": "The fetus derives only from male fluid.", "reasons": "Al-Qurṭubī reports the earlier claim from 77:20, 32:8 and 75:37, and rejects exclusivity in light of this verse."}]}
{"id": "49:13/q03", "question": "What follows from shared creation?", "turns_on": "Whether the main inference is equal status or social fraternity.", "positions": [{"id": "49:13/q03/p1", "position": "People share lineage and human dignity, so ancestry, color and birth confer no superiority.", "reasons": "Al-Jurjānī invokes Adam's dust and a poetic maxim requiring earned merit; Rāzī notes neither birth nor tribal assignment is chosen. ʿAlī's poem contrasts common clay with knowledge and action. Al-Biqāʿī says the sex-specific strengths and weaknesses he mentions confer no status; Ibn ʿAṭiyya stresses equality. Al-Jishumī says human descent antedates religious law."}, {"id": "49:13/q03/p2", "position": "Common origin establishes brotherhood and should stop mockery and backbiting.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī finds this link weaker than the direct rebuttal of lineage pride; Elmalılı recalls the image of eating a brother's flesh."}]}
{"id": "49:13/q04", "question": "What do peoples and tribes denote?", "turns_on": "Whether the terms mark nested lineage, region, or distinct ethnic populations.", "positions": [{"id": "49:13/q04/p1", "position": "Peoples are broader, more remote lineages; tribes are nearer subdivisions.", "reasons": "Muḍar and Rabīʿa are common examples over Tamīm and Bakr; genealogy descends through ʿimāra, baṭn, fakhdh, faṣīla and sometimes ʿashīra. Ibn al-Aḥmar's and al-Kumayt's poetry support the usage; versions differ in lesser ranks. Al-Ṭabarī also transmits the simple gloss 'lineages'; al-Bayḍāwī and al-Zajjāj state the large-to-small order."}, {"id": "49:13/q04/p2", "position": "Peoples are smaller branches below tribes.", "reasons": "Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, Ibn ʿAbbās in one report, al-Ḥasan and Abū Sulaymān reverse the usual ranking. Ibn ʿAṭiyya says the report opposes the cited linguists' consensus."}, {"id": "49:13/q04/p3", "position": "Peoples are non-Arabs or their divisions, tribes Arabs; asbāṭ are Israelite tribes.", "reasons": "Abū ʿUbayd gives the non-Arab gloss; al-Ālūsī cites Masrūq's jizya report and the Shaʿūbiyya association. Al-Bayḍāwī likewise distinguishes non-Arab subdivisions from Arab tribes."}, {"id": "49:13/q04/p4", "position": "Peoples are clients or people without known ancestry; tribes are Arab lineages.", "reasons": "The Ibn ʿAbbās–ʿAṭāʾ report says clients; al-Qushayrī's examples include Indians and Turks. Abū Razīn specifies mountain dwellers."}, {"id": "49:13/q04/p5", "position": "Peoples identify by towns, regions or valleys; tribes identify by paternal descent.", "reasons": "Abū Rāzin and Abū Rawq give towns and villages, al-Māwardī cites poetry, and Sufyān contrasts Himyar with Hijazi Arabs. Rāzī distinguishes dispersed peoples with unknown common ancestor from tribes joined by one known ancestor."}, {"id": "49:13/q04/p6", "position": "Peoples are Yemen's Qaḥṭān descendants; tribes are Rabīʿa, Muḍar and other ʿAdnān descendants.", "reasons": "Al-Māwardī reports this as a second classification."}]}
{"id": "49:13/q05", "question": "What are the roots and forms of peoples and tribes?", "turns_on": "The cited vowel and root usages vary.", "positions": [{"id": "49:13/q05/p1", "position": "Shaʿb evokes branching and gathering, but its root can also mean separating or repairing.", "reasons": "A tree and joining needle illustrate gathering; death is Shuʿūb because it separates. Al-Jishumī quotes ʿĀʾisha about Abū Bakr mending the community. Al-Rāghib compares a valley. Qabīla evokes facing parts of a head."}, {"id": "49:13/q05/p2", "position": "Shuʿūb is plural of shaʿb with fatḥa; shiʿb with kasra is a mountain path, plural shiʿāb.", "reasons": "The Hamdān subclan al-Shaʿb and the nisba Shaʿūbiyya are also noted; Ibn ʿAṭiyya favors an explanation of the latter from broad non-Arab peoples."}, {"id": "49:13/q05/p3", "position": "Qabāʾil is the regular faʿāʾil broken plural of qabīla.", "reasons": "Sībawayh compares ṣaḥīfa and katība and surveys related feminine, weak, geminate, small-count and larger-count plural rules; al-Dāmghānī glosses tribes."}]}
{"id": "49:13/q06", "question": "Why name only peoples and tribes?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "49:13/q06/p1", "position": "They are the furthest lineage divisions people readily recognize; narrower ranks are clearer.", "reasons": "Al-Biqāʿī gives six levels and cites al-Baghawī on the last named ʿashīra."}]}
{"id": "49:13/q07", "question": "Why make peoples and tribes?", "turns_on": "Whether the purpose is genealogical, cooperative, theological or extended by a variant construction.", "positions": [{"id": "49:13/q07/p1", "position": "To recognize ancestry and degrees of kinship and manage relationships, without boasting.", "reasons": "Mujāhid gives the example of knowing whose son someone is. Al-Ṭabrisī adds transactions and hadith transmission; al-Ālūsī adds inheritance; Ibn Kathīr cites a gharīb report about learning kinship; al-Kāshifī distinguishes people with the same name by tribal name."}, {"id": "49:13/q07/p2", "position": "To foster mutual support, cooperation and social cohesion.", "reasons": "Rāzī reports mutual support as another purpose and prefers recognition over estrangement because of 49:11–12. Elmalılı adds affection and protection; Asad stresses appreciation of shared humanity."}, {"id": "49:13/q07/p3", "position": "Recognition of one another points to recognition of God.", "reasons": "Rāzī argues God, rather than a noble ancestor, is the noblest source of honor."}, {"id": "49:13/q07/p4", "position": "The open-hamza reading extends the purpose to knowing that the pious are noblest.", "reasons": "Al-Farrāʾ says li-taʿrifū is more direct, but allows li-taʿārafū; al-Zajjāj and others connect the clauses."}]}
{"id": "49:13/q08", "question": "How is li-taʿārafū read?", "turns_on": "Deletion, preservation or assimilation of the prefix, or a different verbal stem.", "positions": [{"id": "49:13/q08/p1", "position": "The majority elide one original tāʾ.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān and al-Samīn identify the common form; Bursevî spells out contraction."}, {"id": "49:13/q08/p2", "position": "Al-Aʿmash and others preserve both tāʾs.", "reasons": "The full li-tataʿārafū is reported repeatedly."}, {"id": "49:13/q08/p3", "position": "Others assimilate the tāʾs.", "reasons": "Mujāhid, Ibn Kathīr in one transmission, Ibn Muḥayṣin and al-Bazzī are named; the qirāʾāt note says assimilation is phonetic and leaves sense unchanged. Al-Bayḍāwī lists assimilated and unassimilated forms."}, {"id": "49:13/q08/p4", "position": "Li-taʿrifū lacks the alif and derives from ʿarifa.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās and Abān from ʿĀṣim are named, with Ubayy and others in Ibn al-Jawzī; Ibn Jinnī supplies an omitted object such as kinship."}, {"id": "49:13/q08/p5", "position": "Further forms have doubled rāʾ or Ibn Masʿūd's expanded wording.", "reasons": "The Kashshāf includes li-tataʿarrafū; Ibn al-Jawzī names Abū Nuhayk and al-Aʿmash for two tāʾs and doubled rāʾ; Ibn Masʿūd adds 'among yourselves' and 'the best of you'."}]}
{"id": "49:13/q09", "question": "How does li-taʿārafū work grammatically?", "turns_on": "Whether lām is purposive or imperative and whether the verb has an implicit object.", "positions": [{"id": "49:13/q09/p1", "position": "Its lām expresses purpose and attaches to 'We made you'.", "reasons": "Al-Samīn states the attachment; al-Majāz says it completes the prior clause."}, {"id": "49:13/q09/p2", "position": "With li-taʿrifū and open anna, an imperative lām makes anna the object.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya, Abū Ḥayyān and al-Ālūsī prefer this semantically; al-Samīn calls it unlikely."}, {"id": "49:13/q09/p3", "position": "If the lām is purposive with li-taʿrifū, its object is omitted.", "reasons": "Authors supply 'the truth' or kinship; Ibn Jinnī compares poetic ellipsis."}]}
{"id": "49:13/q10", "question": "How is inna akramakum read and connected?", "turns_on": "Hamza vowel and whether the clause is independent or governed by the preceding wording.", "positions": [{"id": "49:13/q10/p1", "position": "The majority use kasra and begin a new sentence.", "reasons": "Al-Farrāʾ says honor is outside the purpose clause; al-Majāz says connection would use open anna; al-Thaʿlabī notes the pause."}, {"id": "49:13/q10/p2", "position": "A reported open anna connects the honor criterion backward.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās is cited; explanations include a reason for not boasting, knowing that the pious are noblest, or the object of imperative li-taʿrifū."}]}
{"id": "49:13/q11", "question": "What does akram mean?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "49:13/q11/p1", "position": "Most noble, honored or excellent in divine rank.", "reasons": "Ibn Qutayba compares karīm in other uses; Ibn al-Jawzī catalogs excellence and superiority."}]}

before God?", "turns_on": "Universal piety criterion versus a specific identification and the distinction between worldly and divine honor.", "positions": [{"id": "49:13/q12/p1", "position": "Piety, obedience and earned virtue, rather than ancestry, wealth, race or status.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī defines duties and avoidance; Rāzī cites 53:39 for earned value; the Farewell reports deny Arab and color privilege. Rāzī allows lineage to matter socially when religion is equal, not before God."}, {"id": "49:13/q12/p3", "position": "Bilāl is the person particularly identified as most honored in the occasion report.", "reasons": "Muqātil names him; al-Wāḥidī transmits this identification."}]}

{"id": "49:13/q14", "question": "Does piety lead to honor or honor to piety?", "turns_on": "Direction of implication in the two elatives.", "positions": [{"id": "49:13/q14/p1", "position": "Greater piety yields greater divine honor.", "reasons": "Rāzī calls this better known, though the reverse more apparent in wording; his sweetness analogy makes the ranks proportional."}, {"id": "49:13/q14/p2", "position": "Being more honored by God brings greater piety.", "reasons": "Rāzī presents this alternative direction."}]}
{"id": "49:13/q15", "question": "Can lineage retain legitimate distinction?", "turns_on": "Whether rejection of boasting also excludes qualified genealogical or social distinctions.", "positions": [{"id": "49:13/q15/p1", "position": "Pedigree alone cannot confer divine rank; one's acquired faith and conduct decide.", "reasons": "Al-Jurjānī's poetic maxim requires one's own merit. Bursevî locates honor in servanthood rather than office."}, {"id": "49:13/q15/p3", "position": "Lineage may have customary or legal standing without determining divine honor.", "reasons": "Rāzī reports the noblewoman/Nabatian objection and answers that religion overwhelms lesser rank. {"id": "49:13/q16", "question": "What does the closing description of God's knowledge add?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "49:13/q16/p1", "position": "God knows outward deeds and inward piety, so He alone knows who deserves honor.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī cites 31:34; al-Nasafī stresses heart's inclinations; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī contrasts God's informed choice with imaginary worldly honor; Islahi says an unknown pious person may outrank a prominent Qurashī."}]}
{"id": "49:13/q17", "question": "What event occasioned this verse?", "turns_on": "Different occasion reports and, within them, differing names, actions and gradings.", "positions": [{"id": "49:13/q17/p1", "position": "Bilāl's call from the Kaaba at Mecca's conquest provoked racial and status objections.", "reasons": "Muqātil names ʿAttāb, al-Ḥārith, Suhayl and Abū Sufyān; Gabriel reportedly disclosed their remarks. {"id": "49:13/q18", "question": "What did the Prophet proclaim at the conquest when citing this verse?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "49:13/q18/p1", "position": "He abolished pre-Islamic ancestral pride: all descend from Adam, while piety or wickedness determines divine rank.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿUmar's route is called gharīb by al-Tirmidhī, and Yaḥyā ibn Maʿīn weakened ʿAbd Allāh ibn Jaʿfar. {"id": "49:13/q25", "question": "What other sūra notices occur with this verse?", "turns_on": "Distinct notices, not competing answers.", "positions": [{"id": "49:13/q25/p1", "position": "In one Medinan chronology al-Ḥujurāt follows al-Mujādila and precedes al-Taḥrīm.", "reasons": "Al-Burhān counts 85 Meccan and 29 Medinan sūras but notes disagreement."}, {"id": "49:13/q25/p2", "position": "A report promises ten good deeds per obedient and disobedient person to its reciter.", "reasons": "Al-Jishumī transmits this from Ubayy ibn Kaʿb."}, {"id": "49:13/q25/p3", "position": "A neighboring notice calls Sūrat Qāf Meccan with forty-five verses.", "reasons": "Elmalılı includes it adjacent to this verse's discussion."}]}

{"id": "50:16/q01", "question": "What does God's creation of the human mean?", "turns_on": "Whether خلقنا refers only to initial formation or to continuing dependence and renewal.", "positions": [{"id": "50:16/q01/p1", "position": "God brought the human into ordered, wise existence.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya defines creation as ordered, measured, wise bringing into being."}, {"id": "50:16/q01/p2", "position": "Human creation and existence are continuously renewed and dependent on God.", "reasons": "Ṭabāṭabāʾī includes ongoing changing existence; the present knowledge clause and enduring nearness accompany it. {"id": "50:16/q02", "question": "Why is human creation stated so emphatically here?", "turns_on": "Whether the emphasis chiefly grounds knowledge of inward states or the resurrection argument.", "positions": [{"id": "50:16/q02/p1", "position": "The emphatic assertion supports the following claim to know hidden human states.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr says lām and qad anticipate the coordinated knowledge clause: people acknowledge creation but fail to grasp God's knowledge. Islāhī argues that the Creator must know every detail of His creatures, including thoughts before words and deeds, since otherwise He could not arrange their protection and sustenance; he cites the question at 67:14."}, {"id": "50:16/q02/p2", "position": "The reminder of first creation establishes the power to recreate people.", "reasons": "Al-Kāshifī says Meccan polytheists admitted the first creation without matter or aid, so resurrection from matter is possible despite Satanic doubt. {"id": "50:16/q03", "question": "Who is ٱلْإِنسَٰنَ here?", "turns_on": "Whether the singular is generic or singles out Adam before generalization.", "positions": [{"id": "50:16/q03/p1", "position": "Humanity generally, especially the addressed polytheists and Adam's descendants.", "reasons": "Al-Wāḥidī, Ibn ʿAṭiyya, Ṭabrisī, Ibn al-Jawzī, Qurṭubī and Study Quran take a generic human; Ibn ʿĀshūr says polytheists are the immediate audience (50:19–22). Al-Dāmghānī and Ibn al-Jawzī compare other generic uses, including 76:2. {"id": "50:16/q07", "question": "What is included in the soul's whisper here?", "turns_on": "The notes distinguish the broad range of inner activity from specific moral, historical, and inward applications.", "positions": [{"id": "50:16/q07/p1", "position": "All private inward speech, thoughts, feelings, intentions and secrets.", "reasons": "Ṭabarī and al-Thaʿlabī say nothing in the heart is hidden. {"id": "50:16/q10", "question": "How can a pronoun be repeated or followed by another pronoun?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "50:16/q10/p1", "position": "A separate pronoun may confirm or stand in apposition to an attached pronoun, subject to its case and construction.", "reasons": "Sībawayh gives بك أنت and رأيتك أنت, distinguishes this from ordinary adjectival description, and uses إياك/إياه for accusative and أنت/هو for nominative apposition. {"id": "50:16/q11", "question": "What does divine knowledge of the whisper establish?", "turns_on": "The notes differ over whether the emphasis merely establishes unlimited divine knowledge or also contrasts it with the angels' limited record.", "positions": [{"id": "50:16/q11/p1", "position": "No inward or outward state is hidden from the Creator, even before its thought emerges.", "reasons": "Ṭabarī, Zajjāj, Thaʿlabī, Wāḥidī, Baghawī and Ṭabrisī stress concealed thoughts. {"id": "50:16/q14", "question": "What does God's being nearer than the jugular mean?", "turns_on": "The dispute turns on whether the first-person plural names God's knowledge or power, both attributes, His angels, or a deeper nonspatial relation; the following angels and the prior knowledge clause are key contextual evidence.", "positions": [{"id": "50:16/q14/p1", "position": "God's knowledge and witness encompass the person more intimately than any physical closeness.", "reasons": "Ṭabarī, al-Naḥḥās, Muqātil, Wāḥidī, Baghawī, Ṭabrisī, Rāzī, Bayḍāwī, Nasafī, Abū Ḥayyān, Biqāʿī, Ālūsī, Elmalılı and Ibn ʿĀshūr make this reading. Bodily parts or flesh conceal one another or the vein, but nothing screens God. Bayḍāwī's close observer and Elmalılı's omitted 'whoever' explain the comparator; one possible observer is the person himself. Al-Itqān applies the rule of interpreting impossible literal attributes by their implication. The image is not spatial presence."}, {"id": "50:16/q14/p2", "position": "God has greater power, mastery and command over the person than the vein.", "reasons": "Reported by Arabic interpreters, Akhfash, Māwardī, Ṭabrisī, Rāzī and Elmalılı. Ibn ʿAṭiyya stresses dominion and grasp without bodily proximity; Rāzī compares command in the person with blood moving through veins. Qurṭubī contrasts the person's control of the vein; al-Ḍaḥḥāk and an Abū Saʿīd prophetic report assert the comparison, the latter joining it to God intervening between heart and person and holding forelocks."}, {"id": "50:16/q14/p3", "position": "The clause conveys knowledge and power together, with care and effects such as kindness or wrath.", "reasons": "Thaʿlabī and Qushayrī join knowledge and power; Muqātil as quoted by Qurṭubī combines both. Elmalılı prefers the combination: power entails knowledge, and the added nearness clause goes beyond the preceding knowledge clause. He weighs the proposed bar on combining metaphors against context cues and says a representative metaphor can unite them. Islāhī says God's knowledge and power encompass each person, both seen and unseen."}, {"id": "50:16/q14/p4", "position": "The near ones are God's angels placed near the human, rather than divine indwelling.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathīr argues from 56:85, where unseen nearness to the dying is angelic, and 15:9, where 'We sent down' acts through angels. God enables angelic prompting alongside satanic prompting; the Prophet likened Satan's movement to blood. Study Quran reports this reading, while noting interpreters seek to avoid literal divine nearness. Ibn Kathīr says the wording does not demand a mere knowledge reading."}, {"id": "50:16/q14/p5", "position": "God is nearer in perception than the jugular would be if it perceived.", "reasons": "Ṭabrisī reports this further gloss."}, {"id": "50:16/q14/p6", "position": "The nearness is a real, abiding ontological relation in which each created self and faculty depends on God.", "reasons": "Qāshānī rejects spatial conjunction but says particular existence stands only through divine existence; he cites ʿAlī that God is with things without conjunction. Ṭabāṭabāʾī says God mediates between soul and itself and actions (8:24), while the familiar image only approximates greater nearness. Ibn ʿArabī, as Elmalılı reports, places the Near One above bodily life channels, makes faculties dependent on God, and describes nearness with distance; devotional nearness through prescribed acts makes God the servant's hearing and sight without identity. Study Quran reads divine immanence throughout creation (2:115, 57:4). Elmalılı accepts essential and active nearness yet insists creation, divine acts, and the servant remain distinct, citing 37:96 and 8:17; unity language must not become union. He says God's encompassing cannot be spatial, and common exegesis uses attributes to prevent that impression."}, {"id": "50:16/q14/p7", "position": "God remains more powerful and knowledgeable than the two recording angels when they arrive.", "reasons": "Study Quran reports a reading tied to 50:17: God needs no angels to know acts. Elmalılı suggests the omitted close comparator could be the recording angels, whom God exceeds in nearness."}]}

{"id": "50:16/q20", "question": "What is the syntax of وَنَعْلَمُ and وَنَحْنُ أَقْرَبُ?", "turns_on": "The grammatical account of how wāw introduces the circumstantial clauses.", "positions": [{"id": "50:16/q20/p1", "position": "وَنَعْلَمُ has an omitted subject, 'and We know'; its nominal clause is circumstantial, as is the nearness clause.", "reasons": "Samīn says a positive imperfect directly joined to wāw cannot itself be the circumstantial clause; the nominal analysis supplies it."}, {"id": "50:16/q20/p2", "position": "The nearness clause is circumstantial to the pronoun in وَنَعْلَمُ and reinforces continuous knowledge.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr treats it as a confirming ḥāl."}]}

{"id": "50:16/q22", "question": "How does the verse fit its neighboring argument?", "turns_on": "The notes connect the verse both to the resurrection proof and to the theological safeguard supplied by creation.", "positions": [{"id": "50:16/q22/p1", "position": "It answers resurrection deniers by moving from creation and God's knowledge to recording, death and requital.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya says these verses prove resurrection and requital. {"id": "50:16/q23", "question": "What responses should awareness of divine nearness evoke?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "50:16/q23/p1", "position": "It produces fear and awe in some, tranquility and intimacy in others, and calls for obedience and remembrance.", "reasons": "Qushayrī gives the contrasting effects; Biqāʿī repeats him. {"id": "50:27/q03", "question": "How can Satan's denial fit a claim that he prepared the person in 50:23?", "turns_on": "How to understand Satan's earlier preparation: causation, embellishment without compulsion, or a boast later withdrawn.", "positions": [{"id": "50:27/q03/p1", "position": "The two claims appear to conflict if Satan's preparation means that he misguided the person.", "reasons": "Razi raises the difficulty when the earlier statement that the person is ready for punishment is assigned to Satan."}, {"id": "50:27/q03/p2", "position": "Satan prepared the path by adorning it, without compelling the person to follow.", "reasons": "Razi reports al-Zamakhshari's reconciliation."}, {"id": "50:27/q03/p3", "position": "Satan spoke at different times: he boasted first, then retracted on seeing shared punishment.", "reasons": "Razi reports al-Zamakhshari's alternative, relating the boast to 38:82–85 and the retraction to the sight of his own penalty."}]}
